blocks.x: Okay, it's going all right Lee.

Oh, it's going? Yeah. Hello, this is Lee Collins talking here. I was born in Deeroux, New Orleans, October 17, 1901. I was raised uptown. I'm almost born with a cornet. My daddy was a cornet player, my grandfather was a cornet player. They played with the old Tio boys, Lorenzo Tio's daddy and his uncle. And I started blowing all my old, my daddy's cornet when I was around about six or seven, six or seven years old. And I kept on playing and playing.
About what street were you born on?
I was born on Della Chaves in Robeson. Oh yes. And I was raised on Losing Avenue between Threatt and Robeson.
Do you remember the first bands you heard or you heard your father?

Yeah, the first good jazz band I heard was the Eagle Band with Bunk. With Bunk. How did you? Bunk was the man that really knocked me out. And the first time I heard Bunk, I got in my head that I wanted to play cornet just like Bunk did. Bunk did. Well Bunk played in the town of Ruffport City. The old funky but all on Padilla Street. Well yeah I took a picture of that. And so there was a great friend of my family, a fellow that called Foots used to work at the parties market. Foots was a bouncer there and Foots used to carry me there and let me hear Bunk play.
Did he really have great big feet I think Bunk told me about it. Yeah he had big feet. Foots was a bouncer and had feet almost big as the funky but all.

Yeah Foots was a great band. Foots was a great band. So Foots was with the Eagle Band and Frankie Dusen and Pache was a little boy that was playing clarinet in this band. So all the guys, when I walked in the place, Foots bought me and they thought I was Frankie Dusen's part because I looked like Frankie at that time. Frankie was slant and they were resembled each other. So they had wore uniforms, I'm going to get them, all them brown uniforms at that time. And I put on Bunk's Eagle cap and picked up his counter and started playing at the animals ball. And I knew he didn't play. How old were you about? I was about ten years old at that time. My aunt and I had moved down on Gasket Street and I was living so far from the funky but all at that time. So my daddy wanted me to be strictly by the music. So I knew practically all the old downtown musicians were musicians like Manuel Perez, they read music but they didn't have that spirit. Those uptown boys had like Joe Oliver and Bunk and all the rest of the boys, another boy they called, Johnson, was no kin to Bunk, was a good cornet player.
Joe Johnson.

Joe Johnson. Joe Johnson. Joe Johnson and Bunk and Buddy Beteete they all played by the same little style. So that kept me going. And so about 1915 I was close to 14 years old. I started playing with the whole Columbia band, the whole Columbia band, a cornet player called Tick Chambers. The band was getting ready to come north and so George Foster was in the band, Pop Foster, and they told him, says the kid uptown in Losing Avenue, play like Bunk, Lee Collins, why don't you give Lee Collins a chance and let him play cornet in this band. So I joined the Columbia band very young, very young. I used to wear Mark Loenis' long pants and coat and to go play in this band and go to school in the daytime, playing the band all night long and go to school in the daytime. Tom LaFont School was not so far from my home where I lived, on Losing Avenue. So about 1915, 16, the Zulu parade, the drummer by the name of Black Benny hired me to play a street parade. And this parade was Louis Armstrong. I had seen Louis Armstrong play before, but I hadn't seen him. The first time I'd seen him play, he was with the Joneses band, they come to play for the dedication of the playground at Tom LaFont, him and Kid Renee at that time. But I had never seen him in a band professional. So Benny hired me for this parade, because the musician was hard to get. I was very young to play for the Zulus. And the band was Louis Armstrong, another corner player by the name of Schatz, and myself. We three played. So that was a great thrill of my life, because I had never played a street parade before. That's a good plan. I had never played a street parade before. It was for a real-age battle house club, the Zulus. So I noticed Louis had a similar touch of bunk too. He was playing on the other bunk, so that just set me right, because it brought my style right to me. So at that time I thought I was really going good. So bunk, bunk was, bunk was playing down the spot jobs around, I think the Eagle band had broken up or something. Tubby Hall and left and went to come to Chicago, he was drumming with him at that time. Bache was playing in the honky tonks, forgot to call tooddle him and grabbing Franklin. So bunk didn't show up on the job once. He was on his little drinking spree. So they come and got me to play in the great bunk's place. So that really made me feel good, not because bunk was drunk, didn't show up, because I had a chance to sub for bunk. I was thinking that I was getting some plays, time to go in, time I was good enough to go in bunk's place, because bunk was the number one corner at that time. Joe Oliver at that time was a butler on Magazine Street. He was playing and coming out and listening to that room. So I had heard, I didn't hear Joe Oliver play until he come to work for Pete Lallers, Pete Lallers Cabaret. Pete Lallers and I was, it was Joe Oliver and Lorenzo Teal, they had a bunch playing together. So I used to go, I was too young to go into the halls, I'd stand outside and listen to Joe. Joe was a little different from the bunk. My man was very powerful, listen to him. So I kept on going, kept on going, kept on going until I, Louis Armstrong, little band, East Comin' the Duckies, little band, was managed by a great friend of mine called little Joe Lindsay. Joe Lindsay is a brown skin jazz band. So I joined Joe Lindsay's band where Louis was playing and Louis was, went in the honky-tonks back at that time and I was playing with little Joe Lindsay's band. So, by that time I got a chance to go, to go work for, go work down in the district, what they call Storyville now. Buddy Petit was working with Jimmy Noon in a place called Few Clothes Place. You heard of that place?
Oh yeah, George Few Clothes.

George Few Clothes Place. So Buddy Petit had joined the tuxedo band with Celestan, then went out to the suburban garden. So I goes out to George Few Clothes in the district and work for, and work where Buddy Petit was playing with Jimmy Noon and that bunch. So, that time, there was coming drafting and drafting for the World War I. Registration was coming around. And the guy was looking for, that didn't register for the war, didn't register to go to war. And the guy asked me, say, let me see your registration card. I was a pretty big boy for my age. I was way older than my age because I was tall and slender and had on them big high waist and long pants with my uncle. So I told him, I said, I didn't have no registration card. I said, I'm not old enough to go to war. And then he said, what you doing here? And he said, and he gave me about three minutes, three seconds to get out. So I got out the district, and I joined Jack Kerrie's band. Jack Kerrie's band, a young Clannett player just had come and just began playing with Edmund Hall. And so Jack Kerrie had had his brother playing, cornered with him, Mud Kerrie, so Mud Kerrie had went with Ory, back with Kid Ory's band. So I got in Jack Kerrie's band and told Jack Kerrie about this young Clannett player that I liked. So Jack Kerrie said, get him. And the Clannett player was Edmund Hall. So we worked with Jack Kerrie. And that time Jack Kerrie was playing Tiger Rag, which was not on wax then, but they was calling it Jack Kerrie, playing old Tiger Rag. But we didn't call it Tiger Rag. So they taught me Tiger Rag, and everybody would play Jack Kerrie. So we was playing spot jobs all around Magazine Street, all the rich jobs, fraternity jobs, and everybody was doing good. I was making quite a bit jack for myself at that time, very young, still was in my teens, still was in my teens, playing cornet. So then I stayed with Jack Kerrie's band for about a year. And I leaves Jack Kerrie's band and joined another band called the Young Tuxedo Band.
You heard of that band? Yeah, they still have one.

It was run by a bass player called Duck Winnie's. So Duck Winnie's had another cornet player in the band, it was Kid Rene. So he was using two cornets, Kid Rene and myself. He was never awful, but powerful cornet player, played very high at that time. So Duck said, Lee, I'm going to leave Rene go because Rene is getting to drinking too much and I think he's going to spoil you and start you drinking. I never was a guy who could drink much whiskey. Anyway, at the time a few drinks I drank, it always made me sick. And it showed up in my plane. So they got rid of Rene so I could get the whiskey away from me. So I played around, played around, played around. So I leaves Duck Winnie's band again and goes back to Jack Kerrie's band because Jack Kerrie had got that job where Joe Oliver and O'Rehead was playing. I grabbed him in Ramport called the Winter Garden. There'd be a place up there. Did you hear about that place? Upstairs.
Upstairs. Upstairs. There's a Pythian temple they call it sometime I think.

I go to work with Jack Kerrie and say, see y'all just quit too early. We went to my place where we used to go, we called Eagle Saloon. We were running by Ben Dale at that time. Ben Mulligan I meant to say. Say, I'm going to work now at the Winter Garden. And so I gets back with Jack Kerrie band and get Edmund Hall. We go back to Jack Kerrie and start playing. So I had quite a ball around the Winter Garden. All the best class musicians to come and sit in. Lorenzo Teal, Buddy Petit was the king, best young corner player then in New Orleans. Because Bunk had been going out and went to the country at that time. You're a place called New Iberia.
How did Buddy Petit play? Buddy Petit played the semi, just like Bunk.

I couldn't tell the difference between him and Buddy, him and Bunk. Buddy Petit was the corner player that really knocked me out. He really, he really, none of our comments playing like between Buddy and Bunk. Buddy Petit was the corner player that had a great big tune and a beautiful soul. And he played with a great drive. He didn't play many high notes, but he didn't need to make no high notes. The way that guy played in the scales was everything. He played with really, he didn't need to make no high notes. So Buddy was very good. So Buddy taking a light to me, he said, kid, he say, he called me then Little Lee. Everybody used to call me Little Lee. He said, Little Lee, you really knocked me out. He said, you're doing good. He said, you put me in my old bunk. I said, well that's my man, that's the guy I wanted, that's the guy like to play like Buddy was Bunk. So he said, that's the guy I come by too, Bunk. He said, Bunk and Joe Johnson, that was the man that knocked me out. So I went to the garden and I go to work. That time on a place they called on Decatur Street. It was run by a little Spanish guy. Decatur, it was on Decatur's out there around by the French market. And it was about three players. We had a white guitar and a white piano player, the boy by the name was Sidney Adrian, but later recorded with me with this story, a story band I think I said. So Sidney Adrian and his guitar player, he was an unknown guitar, I'd like to remember his name, but he was a very good guitar player. He worked piano and drum. He was just a picked up band. That's why I say old New Orleans had mixed bands, I think before they ever thought of that, and nobody paid a bit of attention to it. So Sidney Adrian and I would play together. That's where Sidney Adrian used to play this number. What's this number he composed when he sold it to Carmichael? Lazy River. Lazy River. Lazy River. He used to play it and mug it every time he got drunk. He used to play, because he got that inspiration, he used to go sit on the river every morning and blow his clarinet and look at the river and then the river was kind of lazy that time of the morning coming into Carmichael. He used to play that piece, Lazy River. And I used to play it with him. I was way back there before Lazy River ever think that I would, when I seen the musical Lazy River, I learned Lazy River. All I did was sit in his piece right away. So Bill, we played in this little job, then the war was on. The 1917 war was on. And made little things different, musicians, half of them was, because they had a lot of work or fight. Some of them was working, but I never did work, because I always knew all the little hiding places outside the district where you could go, I could go hide in my corner and play. So, I stayed awake. Well, one time I did try to wake. Joe Lindsey and Louis Armstrong carried me, we all made up, Louis was waking out there, and they all made up their mind to go to wake. Louis was to go to wake, and they carried me out there, and I seen how hard the wake was before I could start, and I slipped off. What sort of a job was it? Oh man, it was rolling cement up there, with a ship building, building ships, building ships. And I was, shucks, I didn't get it for a $50 a day, I didn't want no part of it, because I still love my own. I didn't want to stay away from that long, that long way from my corner. So, I got away from that way.
You want to rest a minute?
Yeah, you better rest.
Why don't you rest a minute? Yeah. Yeah, it's going all right now again.
I thought me and that guy, even dogs are like him.
Yeah.
I believe there's something down there in New Orleans, that climate that makes a man ho. You know, I was very young, that light car climbing. You ready?
Yes, it's going, it's all right now.
It's all right at all?
Yeah, go ahead now.

So Bill, so Bill playing that corner, really was my life. I lived that life, I lived that life and I loved it. Well, what you really got yourself a reputation playing corner in New Orleans was playing in the brass bands, parades. On those parades, you met everybody and the corner players all had their cutting contests. So, I played in the brass band, in Black Penny's brass band with Louis, Renee and myself, regular. And later years, I worked with the Tuxedo band with Papa Celestan. That's where I got, come and get some of my best technique of good old funeral marches we used to play. Good old funeral marches and then, and then, every six eighths, like, Gettysburg march, you know, for the parades and everything. In those days, everybody second line and picked out their band, who they liked, who they liked, who they liked to be and then, and you got famous by that. It's a funny thing, you played in an orchestra, people paid no attention to you, but as soon you hit that street, everybody had their eyes on you, you know, especially those good play cornets. They didn't watch nobody but the cornets and the drums and the clarinet. So, I got to work with a boyfriend of mine, I'm raised up with, Boy Lumprey. Lumprey boys. One of them was a drummer, a poise lady, a lady come to be a cornered player, I helped him out, his grandfather taught him, grandfather taught me a while, the music too. Then Willie Humphrey Client, so, we mix up a band, we mix up a band together, and we played around together a long time, we went to the old Avila dance hall, when I was built between McGonagall and Rampart, next to the 4N, that little Eddie Miller, the Client, Eddie Miller, the saxophone player, he used to play, he used to come in and sit in with me every night there. Then I, I went to work at Canal and Crotlet, with the bass tuba player of the Tuxedo Brass band, Eddie Jackson. Stayed up there a long while playing cornered. One of the greatest things of my life, around 1924 I got a letter from Joe, Joe, Joe Oliver. Yeah, Preston Jackson and, uh, and uh, we tell that boy played drum, play trombone Mary, come here and see me. You got to tell me little brother Montgomery?
They all went. They all went.

They was kids then, just learning how to play trombone at that time. 1924, I got a letter from Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver was telling me that Lewis had quit him and was, was, had gone to work to Dreamlin, but was talking about leaving and going to New York City. And he'd say, uh, Lorenzo Teo had wrote and told Joe Oliver about the progress that I was making on my cornered, cause Joe had asked, who's all the battle house cornered players down there that could play like bunk and uh, all the good old boys. Lorenzo told him, say, Lee Collins is about the best they got in jazz down here now. So Joe wrote me a letter and asked me, how about, how would I like to come to Chicago to work at the Lincoln Garden? He would hear me say, he said, I couldn't, I couldn't hardly finish, I didn't even finish reading the letter. I said, could I come to Chicago to work with him? I stopped reading the letter. So I went right on the way. That, at that time, I talked it over to my first wife at that time and asked her, I say, I got a chance to go to Chicago with Joe Oliver, what, how about me, what you think about me going to jail? And she got knocked out about it. She said, Jesus, we both, we walked around in a daze for about an hour before we could say anything. So I go, I make some beeline right from the Western Union. And I go to the Western Union, I send Joe a telegram and tell him I sound like very much to come to Chicago, join him at the Lincoln Garden. So Joe Oliver looked like before I could get back home I had a ticket there. Joe got the telegram and he said, send me a ticket, told me to come at once. So I go to Chicago, first time, and to play with Joe. So I go to Chicago with Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds and all of them had to quit Joe at that time. They were Baby Dodds and they was working down at Kelly's table, and Johnny Dodds, let me tell you about that.
Yeah, and where was your job?

Yeah, they was working down there and there. Where was Joe playing then? Joe was playing in Lincoln Garden. Lincoln Garden. Louis was working at the Dreamland, and joined the band at the Dreamland. I mean Lil was working there together. So I come to Chicago and I joined Joe's band. Well Joe had George Fields and he had a big band. He had the kind of band that he had now. He had a corner player playing with a man by the name of Bob Schaffner. He went later to the plantation with Dave Payton. So with the band playing, they was playing all the good old tunes from New Orleans. So Joe come down and talked to me on a, Lincoln Garden was packed in jam, King Jones was announced at that time, and he was jumping. Preston Jackson and then a little drum roll player, what's his name again? Al Wynn. Since I've been sick I can't think of nobody's name. Al Wynn, they put me over there in Lincoln Garden. So Joe say, Joe always was a nasty talker you know, Joe put me in the dozens and say, I heard you was there, I heard you could blow. He said, Tio told me you're a human being. I laughed and I laughed and I said, well Joe you know, I can't play like you but I play. He said, what numbers do you know all those numbers you know you've been playing up there? I said, well I know all the standards like Panama and the high society. I know all the good old New Orleans tunes and all the standards. He said, when you be here tomorrow at two o'clock they will have rehearsal. So I stayed to the last note that Joe was playing. I still couldn't sleep. I went home living on Cottage Grove in 3030 at that time, 3310 Cottage Grove. I went home I couldn't sleep because the thrills were thinking that he could sit by the King, King Oliver that time. See, so I went and Joe called Roycele and after we run down about three tunes Joe stopped Roycele and said, well that's enough. He said, you got a tuxedo suit Lee? I said, no man. He said, I ain't got no tuxedo. He said, well I'll just wear your dark suit. He said, be to work tonight. He said, you start to work tonight, 85 a week. 85, I never had any great great 85 a week. I made it, but I never had that kind of salary. Jesus have mercy. 85 a week. I said, so I go to work with Joe and Joe was tickled to death and everything. I said, I'm alright Papa? He said, you're alright. So he said, what you want tomorrow? You come and get them red beans and rice. I have Stella to cook your nice dinner Lee. He said, come on over. He said, I went over there and so Miss Stella met right at the door with smiles and he said, Lee? He said, you Lee here? He said, I said, yes. He said, Joe, Joe, I'm so glad. He said, you made Joe feel good. Joe's sleeping now, but he's going to wake up. He said, Joe, you made Joe feel good by it. He said, Joe says he's happy now. He got a boy sitting inside him. He's just like Lewis plays and he said, the old New Orleans stuff is happy again. So I was glad to hear that. And so we got up and Joe and Oliver and Joe say, well, you sure surprised me, Lee. I said, I'm glad Joe because I really want to play with you. He said, I said, great thrills of my life to come to you in this big time and especially in Chicago. And Joe said, don't worry. You'll be with me a long time, Papa. So we went seven nights a week over gardens. So I went over there cleaning to the gardens caught a fire. The garden on a Christmas Eve night. The gardens had caught a fire. I'd been in with Joe about seven, eight months at that time. And frankly saved all my money I had made. It's all but with the rent I was paying. I saved a few hundred dollars and I never had that kind of cash saved. So Joe say, Joe called me home and said, well, he said, they haven't got that garden ready yet. He said, but I got a chance to go on another good job. He said, what's the good musicians back home? He said, it's going to be a big band. And that time I told him about Lewis Russell. I told him about the drummer, Bob Rand, Bonnie Big Eye. I told him about them. So they come up and Joe sent for them. So we started hoisting for the, going to the plantation. It was going to be Joe Oliver and myself in the old plantation. So, and another corned player because they had a big show. Bob Schaffner, we'll use three corneds. Bob was going to play the show down for us. So it was a pretty tough winter that winter. Oh, I had never seen so much snow in all my life. I was wanting Jesus. I was falling down, walking through that slope, going to rehearsal. And I was disgusted because it's so cold. My heart is freezing up the bowels. I get there to warm up.
So I said, when did y'all go home?

Joe and Joe say, we go to work in three weeks. So I got the blues for old New Orleans, the old gang, the good old street parades and all the good old places where we used to play at. So I slipped off from Joe and went back, bought me a ticket and went back home, went back to New Orleans because I had improved all night on my cornet and technique was better and everything was better by playing with all fine musicians too. Old Joe had filled on that trombone. So I go back. Oh, it was the thrills of their life that I had to come back to New Orleans and I told them about Joe Oliver and played with Joe and everything. So I go to work at that time back in New Orleans, the place called Entertainers. With a very good piano player, Bill I wish you'd heard him, you knocked him out. A boy from Kansas City called Udell Wilson.
Oh, I heard, yeah, Manuel Moneta talking about it. And Manuel Moneta was in the band.
Udell Wilson, Inez Trepani on drum, a boy called Georgie Boy, a clarinet, they're all dead now. All but Manuel. Manuel looked fine last time I said it.
Well he said to tell everybody how low for him too. Yeah, they look good, Manuel did. He's pretty heavy, but he's good health though.

And I go to work in Astoria, I mean entertainers, playing this band. And this was a band, that time was the talk of New Orleans. We kept it everything. Packed and jammed every night. Fake Marbles band was in there. And I got Zooty's wife's brother, Cornet Flair.
Cornet Flair.

Cornet Flair would come and sit in Whitville. And things was going good, things was going good. Oh man, I was feeling fine. I didn't miss Chicago at all because I was back home, where the jazz played like I liked to hear it. And everybody was playing so good around New Orleans at that time. But a man, he was playing. But a man, he was playing. He had burned himself out of whiskey then. He wasn't doing so good. So he came in there. So he came in there.
So he came in there. So he came in there. So he came in there. So he came in there. So he came in there. So he came in there.

I mean entertainers, playing this band. And this was, this was band, that time was the talk of New Orleans. We captained everything. Packed and jammed every night. We'd make novels bands in there. Judy's wife's brother, Cornet Creft. Cornet Creft would come and sit in with them. And things was going good. Things was going good. Oh man, I was feeling fine. I didn't miss Chicago at all because I was back home, where the jazz played like I liked to hear it. And everybody was playing so good around New Orleans at that time. Buddy my man, he was, but Buddy himself out on whiskey then. He wasn't doing so good. So he come in, he's a very sensitive guy. He come in to play some.
Oh, you were talking about the Buddy fatigue when he came in.

Buddy come in, and he hadn't heard me since I left. He hadn't heard me since I come back from Duolst. So, I asked Buddy to play a bit, play. Come and sit in and play. So Buddy come and sit in, so he didn't play so well at that time. He didn't play the effects of whiskey had really brought him down. It sounded like a different corner to play altogether. So, Manu Mineta was a very sensitive guy too. He wanted me to come back and take that horn back and play. So, I just, so I hated to do this. I had to ask Buddy, I'll come back and play. So Buddy sat on the bandstand, he looked at me, Bill, and he made my start drinking. I had to drink because I had drunk because he made me feel bad. He started crying. He said, Lee, he said, I'm so glad to see you playing like that. He said, you put me on myself now like I used to play. I said, Buddy, you play good shit. You play good shit, Buddy. I play good shit, Buddy. So, I play as long as entertainers, entertainers, entertainers, and I come as to make a very, very good name for myself playing that. I got tangled up with it. You know, I take it easy, Bill. I take it easy because it's my better day today. I guess it may be one of my last good auditions of talking.
You want to turn it off for a minute, Lee? No, you got to turn it off for a minute. Okay. Yeah, it's going again now, Lee.

So, this entertainer was run by two Sicilians, Johnny Latters and Joe Latters. Used to be named Old Hunt and One Ranch where Joe Oliver used to play. Yeah. And all the good boys in the good old days. Packed every night, packed every night. We'd close everything down in that part. So, I got tangled up. I can tell it now because it's a long time, it's been a long time. I got tangled up with all the awful friends, girl that time. My name was Albertine. And so, everybody was telling stories at that time about birthdays. That's how I'm coming to get off the corner at the trumpet. So, I said, like, I said, you know, one thing, Monday's my birthday. And this was in the, it wasn't nearby, the spring of the year. My birthday's in October. I said, this is my birthday. I'm getting a birthday. So, Manuel Moneta, saxophone plays away from Welleheim selling them mincebers, selling them bayonetbers. So, they want to know, the girl wants to know what to buy, the people left their friends. So Manuel Moneta say, you better get him a good cornet, a good trumpet. He said, get that short cornet out of his hand and get him a long trumpet. So, they went down and bought me an artist model bushel from the prettiest trumpet that I've seen in my life. And that was my birthday, slipped it in my chair, got me off to the bar to get a glass of gin and Big John to serve me some gin and say, when I come back, the band hit Happy Birthday and presented me this trumpet. And I put the cornet down and I've been playing, 24, 25. I started playing the trumpet.
1925. Yeah.

So, I played the entertainers quite a while, about two years. I leaves and go to Dallas, Texas. And Professor Cook, Professor Cook, who's a dance, dancing man, Charleston man. We go there and we take the band, we made a nice little round there. And I come on back to New Orleans and I went to Wake to see what bands I went to Wake with. I think I made up a band of my own. I went back to the La Vida Club and I leave there and go on that story with David Jones' band. David Jones was the greatest, one of the finest musicians that I've worked with in my life. Oh, that man was a great. He could play sax cornet. He could play anything as good as anybody. So, that story, how they eat. That's why I went to the Test Story Band. I started, we recorded that band. I went and got my boy that played clarinet with me, Sidney Atkins. That played with me.
And you had another clarinet in there before or not?

Yeah, with clarinet. There was a little, well, they weren't much clarinet players. The alto saxophone players played a little clarinet. Wiggles they called it. Poirier. Poirier to hell. So, we go to Wake. We go to Wake in Estoria. And so, I take a little Danny Barker. I had a band, put him in. He never played music. I brought him music well. We go up there and I went to Wake for Beansy. And I stayed up there and clean until I joined Lou Russell's band, New York. Saratoga Club. 29, I leave New Orleans and go to New York City with Russell's band. Russell's band, I come back here and went with Dave Payton's band, Regal Theater. Dave Payton's band, I've been on my own around Chicago ever since.
Yeah.

But, there was no happy days in the world of playing like the good old New Orleans days. When they had that good old real ragtime funky jazz music day. But the funny thing Bill, New Orleans ain't got it no more. They ain't got the jazz. I don't know. Young kids, young boys don't look like they go, they don't want to fall in those timers shoes. They don't play that kind of music. They have a different style. But the other boys, like my boy Tony Peretti, another good boy, they all trying to carry the traditional New Orleans on. They're all trying to go for that jazz band. And I really think that true jazz music is great old American music will never get old. Oh, sorry. Never get old. And my, what a good feeling in my life, with my wife right there, little Mary, little Mary. Oh, now I got a chance to go to Europe. Oh, yes. That European trip was a great experience for me. He played with Mez and who else was in the band? Mez Row. Zutty Singleton, the great jazz that I think would always say, regardless of his disposition, he's the greatest jazz drummer in the world. But Zutty, I want to hear some old, did you hear any old records I made with Mez? Uh-huh.
I heard of you.
I was doing a drive, and then my help fill my ten bands, going from voice to voice.
What band you play with in France? Uh-huh. The French boys.
Yes. What French boys, baby?
Well, you're going to the band that you played with there in France, with men, the musicians in the band. Is that Claude Luther or which band?
No, Claude Luther was...
Well, we played with French men. Was a good saxophone player, good piano saxophone, put me on the Covenhock. What was that boy's name, Mary?
Gilly Feet.
Gilly Feet. Gilly Feet. And the piano player? The piano player was... What piano player? The piano player was a boy named, what's his name again? Claude Bowling.
Claude Bowling.

Oh, yes. He has a band of his own sometimes. He played just like oil hives in oil good days. Really? The sound is like oil. That was my jazz piano player, oil hives. When I say oil hives, I'm caught in a whole lot of territory. So...
Lee, we don't want to bother you with any more questions. I think that covers your life pretty well there.
Yeah, that's...
But...
I'd love to live to play again, Bill. Well, I think you can. I know, Bill. I'd love to see you sitting up here.
I don't think I'll ever play no more. Your voice is good and strong, as strong as ever, I think.

Yeah, but I feel bad at all times. I'm going to say this to my great old friend Barbara Reid. Hello, Barbara. I sure love to live to see you again, babe. From the good old days at the Victory Club. When you and Bill and the gang would come to see, would knock me out. Would do me all the good. You people was a great inspiration to me. And I always think of you, Barbara. I haven't seen you since the good old days up in the... Where I played for the Jazz Club. The Roosevelt Hotel. So... Be sweet. Hope to see you some good old days. Your old friend Lee Collins. And don't forget little Mary. Mary won't tell you hello there. Tell her all, Mary.
Hello, Barbara. I wish you were here with us. And we often talk about you.
She had a lot of fun in those days.
Yes, we did. She had a lot of fun in those days. ¶¶
¶¶ Mr. Willie Linesmith. I called him, I said, Mr. Lion or Mr. Mouse. Oh, you should read this letter. Did you send a copy?

Huh? Did you send a copy yourself? No, I mean, but I mean. Do you still have a copy of what you're sending? Oh, no, I didn't pay no attention to that. You should have made a carbon copy. Yeah, sure. That should be coming up.

Oh, I just woke the man, I told him, I said, man, I've been buying your magazine for 15 years. I said, please, I actually have a special favor. Please print this letter for me. Mr. Mouse. Man, the boy I drug with. I sure hope he puts it up. He pointed me up, you know what I mean. I just hate to see a man talk that way about another man. You know what I mean. You don't have to talk that way about him.

When he tried to copy, he stole his jelly piece of him and he was a finger buster. He couldn't even play it. He put his name down and composed it. He used to play with Sidney Bichet. I don't know how to really hurt him, I guess, in New York, out on Long Island. They played with Sidney Bichet. I don't know who else. I don't know. Maybe.

I put one line in there. It got a part in there about they didn't know how to wear their pegs. I told him, I said, in the joints in Storyville where Janice sat and played, I said, you couldn't even come in the joint because they didn't find out how much lying you was. Did you ever hear him play down here at all? No, no. See, before he died, about eight months before he died, I lived with him and his wife for nine months in New York. I never knew him before, but when I went to New York, I made a point in my mind that I was going to see him. So he was living on 130 feet between 7th and 8th Avenue at a woman's house near New York. She had a rooming house up there. And Janice was living with a woman they called Mabel. Mabel Morton. Now he was, and he wrote a number for her called Posse Mabel. Well, I mean, I had it all night. Him and her, I, her and him used to go to a church every Sunday. Well, I really thought that he was his wife until after his death in California when young comes some man needed somebody. Yeah, man needed, yeah. So I didn't know who, how, how this whole situation was complicated, you know. But I always knew it ought to be Mabel Morton. Yeah. And, uh, I lived in the same house with him, I mean, and I was just with him every day. I went down on the Clarence Williams off. No, he was an erratic cat, man. You know what I mean? Oh, man, he knocked me out. You know what I mean? Yeah. Well, you see what it is. And so, you see what bring about a jealous way is, I mean, they were quite queer to a lot of people. But I understand him thoroughly because for the simple reason why he, he was the George Gershwin of his day. You got to give the man the recognition that he would really, but, but he wanted it so bad and looked like that he just couldn't attain the objective. He wanted to see his name in lights more than anybody you know. He just, he just loved fame. He just loved being the top man. He wasn't going to play second fiddle for nobody. You could bet that. And he'd get up on Broadway and they'd go to talking about various forms of music. Various forms. Well, what do you mean? There isn't but one music, jealous music. Yeah, it's all jelly roll. Boy, he used to knock me out there. That's what you mean, various forms. There's only one music, jelly rolls music.
Did you get along with him all right?

Yeah, I got along with him fine. He used to have a white boy who comes to the house every day. He's a great writer. Him and I got to be good friends. His name is Charles Edward Smith. Yeah, I can say that. Boy, he was crazy about jelly. He was that, man, he was, and Mabel could cook all kind of Creole gumbo and everything. We had us a ball every day up there. I got a manuscript he gave me with a number. I was trying to figure, Mr. Russell, when you said finger breaker, I've got that manuscript, jelly, give it to me. That sounds right. Yeah, I've got it home on a piece of manuscript paper. About seven or eight bars of the piano solo. And it's got jelly roll more than his name on it. He's right when he said jelly roll there.

Yeah, I don't have the record here anymore. I'll bring it down to Missouri. You sure you didn't have it in that pile that we picked out the other night? No, I didn't see it. You never didn't get those records.
I'm surprised you ain't got those records, Mr. Russell.
I got it up in Missouri.
I mean, you know, when you get the story of his life.
About the bad men.
Yeah, we got them. You got them? Yeah. Oh, man. I thought you said you had five of them or something.
I got the whole set.
They're coming out on singles, eh?
They're coming out, no, on a set of 12. You can buy them singles, I think. I shipped five, six of them today. They're on Riverside now. They had been on, there's one of them. What have they been on?
Bad men ballad. That's what I'm talking about.

The Alabama Bound. Yeah, that's the set. Oh, yeah. We're going to play some of those, George. What were they on before? Well, they came out first on circle. Those are the circles. I see. Because I noticed Riverside's doing a lot of re-dubbing. Yeah, and now Riverside's bringing them out.

You see, that's why I tell you this whole supposition is based on envy. Now, do you think these people would do it? It costs a whole lot of money to make a wrecking. Or let this old kid out of something. Matter of fact, the wrecking got to put out a whole lot of money. Now, you think that people would put out all this money on a man who they wouldn't believe should be driving a truck? Boy, that guy's blowing me up, man. You know what I mean?

Yeah. You said Willie. I thought of him as a saxophone player. No, there's a Willie. I thought he was that voice, too. This guy is an old time. Yeah, I've heard of him, too. You know, the funny thing is, he claims he's Jewish. He's darker than you are. You may be many. You should have seen him around the world. He's, I don't know what to say. There's a group of Negroes in Harlem that claim they're not Negroes, and they claim they're Jewish. Yeah, yeah. Now, I don't know what to think of it, but anyway, they've got a big theory.
Well, he follows a religious cult known as, or. Whether they were. Yeah. Well, I mean, they've got some black Jews in Israel, you know.
Well, actually, the Jews came to Africa.
But I ain't going to want them willing to lie and spit.

Anyway, he claims he's Jewish. He gave me a big line that time about that he's really Jewish. Now, maybe he is a Jewish religion, because it's more of a religion than a race. Uh-huh. But first, the Jews came originally from Africa, some people say anyway. They don't know where the whole human race originated down there someplace. Maybe around Egypt or someplace. Or else over in Babylon. They don't know for sure. I don't think. But anyway, Willie the Lion, I remember, told me that he's really not a Negro. He's Jewish. Well, I mean. But.
I know he's a prejudiced kid.
Yeah, he's prejudiced. That's right.

I'm not trying to stand by saying he's a Jewish. I never read of an opinion so biased in my life, you know, because of. Now, you see, but it's one thing, though. You know what you're going to find. You're always going to find that it's mediocre talent that talks that way. I'm a Christian. You see, if they'd have asked Duke Ellington about jelly, if he wouldn't have gave him no great ovation, he still wouldn't have brought him down the drain. Duke would have said, well, yeah, it sounds like great music for its time. Or something like that. You know what I mean? Now, here's one of the greatest individual Negro artists in the world. The Duke. He's got enough composition that he can sit up here and play him all this week in his own right. Now, I mean, he's never been once charged with piracy or stealing nobody's tunes or nothing like that. But that is the kind of people that's going to give you just what you are and what you deserve. But it's always going to be willing to mouse and stuff like that. Oh, boy. I wish that man printed that letter. That man printed that letter will be the most disappointed cat. But you write it. You're not writing. When? I wrote it, oh, about two weeks ago. Mr. Russell, would I be asking too much to play this?
No. I want to hear a bad man about it. I want to see if you want to talk about Aaron Harris. Yeah, well, it's not one of you. Yeah, this is Aaron. That was a bad boy. Did you?

I knew him. Yeah. You knew him too, huh? Oh, yeah, I knew him. What do you think they're talking about? It was a punk like him. It was Toodlam. It was Aaron Harris. It was Frenchy. Oh, it was Johnny Ray. It was Tom Leon. I mean, these were bad boys. You see, when the cop wanted Aaron, they wouldn't take him up like they'd pick up nobody. They'd tell him the chief want to see him. Yeah. I'll be there tomorrow, tell him. They tricked him out of his life. You see, uh... Yeah, they tricked him out of his life. If God's out of heaven, when they would go gambling, they always had a pistol. But they used a pistol for a pawn to get money. But he pawned his pistol on a game one night, and somebody got two of him. Oh, what did God, man. They had been in an alley. Killed him right there back in the alley. In the street. Yeah. Stole his life. Yeah. Stole his life. Yeah, this is your door.
That'd be a gentleman to make it. Yeah, the gentleman, I see.
Well, I figured you would have those. I was down to the street man.

Well, I believe there was Harris. Yeah. The most most of this man I've ever, ever, ever seen. I know him plays me. I really didn't know the man until I had known him for quite a while. He used to love to play pool. That's good. And I was supposed to be a very good pool player. So every day he used to play me for $2. It was really his object. And the state in the police. The state in the police. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Thank you.
